The Harvest Assize was always held on the Carrow Ford bridge, because the bridge belonged to no single house and so to everyone. A long table had been set across the middle of it, and behind the table sat the magistrate from the county town, a tired man in a fur collar who wanted to be home before dark. The whole town stood crowded at both ends of the bridge. Osric stood before the table with the toll-house ledger under his arm. Maren stood a step behind him, pale, her hands folded, looking at no one.

Osric spoke well. He spoke of the tragedy, of the child lost to the Reach, of the grieving mother who could not bear to speak for herself. He spoke of the ford, which needed a keeper, and of the charter, which by law passed to the household when the line was ended. The magistrate nodded along, already reaching for the wax. I ask only, Osric said, that the Assize record the girl as dead, and the charter as ours.

Then someone at the far end of the bridge began to shout, and the crowd parted, and Ailis walked out of it.

She was filthy. There was river mud to her knees and ash in her copper-red braid, and she carried the brass lantern in one hand and a roll of charcoal-black paper in the other. Tamsin walked one step behind her, and a murmur went through the town at the sight of the old woman they had told their children was dead. Ailis did not look at them. She did not look at her mother. She walked to the magistrate's table and set the lantern down on it, very carefully, the way she had hung it on the hook by the toll-gate every evening of her life.

I am not dead, she said. My mother walked me into the Reach on the night of the first frost and told me to wait. I waited. She did not come back. Behind Osric, Maren made a small sound, like a breath taken and never let go.

The silence on the bridge was so complete that you could hear the river underneath it. Osric recovered first. He laughed, and called her a confused child, and said the old madwoman had filled her head with stories. He reached for the rubbing in her hand.

And the light changed.

The grey one came down out of the low cloud and landed on the parapet at the end of the bridge, so heavily that the old stones groaned and the magistrate's ink pot slid off the table. Her ash-grey scales ran with river mist. The bronze band on her horn caught the evening sun. People screamed and fell back against each other. And at the far end of the bridge, Osric's men, who had been guarding the charter chest, drew their bows and aimed at the dragon's throat.

Ailis felt it then, the thing Tamsin had warned her about in the hut. The heat under her collar was no longer gentle. It was a question. The dragon's eyes were fixed on the archers, her jaws had opened a fraction, and deep in her chest a sound was building like a forge being woken. All Ailis had to do was nothing. All she had to do was let it happen, and every person who had stood by while she was sent into the dark would learn what fear was.

She thought of her mother walking away without turning around. She thought of how easy it would be. Then she turned to face the dragon, raised one hand, and said, No. Stay.

The grey one closed her jaws. She lowered her head until her chin rested on the stones of the bridge, and she did not move again.
